title: How To Handle Students Who Are Too Cool To Participate
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the demoralizing experience of introducing a well-planned lesson to eye rolls, sighs, and a too-cool-for-school reaction, arguing that this apathy is a mirage rather than students' true feelings, driven variously by social-media numbness, disbelief that learning can be fun, or peer pressure to seem detached. His core advice is to 'plow on' regardless — proceed with full commitment and determination as if there were no naysayers, because backing down or matching students' low energy guarantees the lesson fails. He offers one concrete tweak for classes with a strong too-cool attitude: double down on modeling, describing and demonstrating exactly what students will do in excessive detail so they can picture themselves succeeding before starting, combined with a crisp 'go' signal rather than a vaguer prompt. If participation still stalls, he recommends stopping immediately and reteaching with even more detail and enthusiasm rather than abandoning the activity.
points: Student too-cool-for-school apathy toward a lesson is usually a mirage, not their true feelings — often driven by social media numbness or peer pressure to seem detached.
'Plow on' regardless of eye rolls or groans; matching students' low energy or backing down guarantees the lesson fails.
Double down on modeling before a lesson prone to too-cool reactions, describing and demonstrating in excessive detail so students can picture themselves succeeding.
Use a crisp, specific 'go' signal rather than a vaguer prompt like 'you may begin' — it gets students moving more urgently and successfully.
If participation still stalls, stop immediately, return to the moment before the 'go' signal, and reteach with even more detail, commitment, and enthusiasm.
quotes: But just as you begin explaining to your class what they’ll actually be doing, you see eye rolls. You hear sighs and groans.
But what your students are showing you—the malaise, the indifference, the apathy—isn’t really who they really are. It’s a mirage whose source varies by student.
Realize the lie, ignore the negativity, and ramp up your determination to teach your awesome lesson anyway. Pretend you have not one naysayer.
The tweak is to double-down on modeling. Be excessive in detailing verbally and demonstratively what exactly they’ll be doing.
You also want to make sure you use the “go” signal. The word “go” gets students moving more urgently and successfully than a manufactured sound or “you may begin.
If they’re still acting too cool to a level that ruins the activity, then stop immediately, return to the moment before saying go, and reteach.
